title: Micah's Idolatry and the Migration of Dan

date.label: Undated Judges narrative
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: Judges 18 narrates Danite seizure and renaming of Laish as Dan
claims.evidence: Judges 18:27–29 (Hebrew Bible, Judges 1–21, Masoretic text, read in full in Hebrew and JPS English via Mechon Mamre). The Danites attack Laish, burn the city, rebuild it, and rename it Dan after their ancestor. Textual description only; the narrated event is not externally corroborated.

claims.claim: Tel Dan is a strongly supported identification for Dan/Laish; excavated settlement sequence cannot name Danite attackers or establish an exact Judges 18 event.
claims.evidence: Biblical Archaeology Society, "City of Dan" overview, Biblical Archaeology website: the identification of biblical Dan at Tel Dan is treated as certain in the site literature, on the parallel between the Arabic name Tell el-Qadi, "the judge," and the name Dan, "judge," on Eusebius placing Dan near Paneas, and on a Greek-Aramaic inscription found on the mound reading "to the god who is in Dan." Kaniewski et al., Tel Dan study, Science Advances (2017), supplementary materials, Table S2, peer-reviewed: the site's Iron I sequence (Strata VI–IVA) with dates, character, and ranked demises; the table states the site's absolute chronology is equivocal. Daniel M. Master, review of DAN IV: The Iron Age I Settlement, American Journal of Archaeology (2021), peer-reviewed: the excavator Avraham Biran's methods were problematic and ethnic or political identity cannot be inferred from material culture without clear contemporary texts. (JCL-10-002's registry source_ids is S012, which was not read and does not enter sources[] — see review.notes; the claim is grounded by BARDan, Kaniewski, and Master2021.) The settlement sequence supports the association — a real, substantial Iron I town stood at the site — but no stratum names Danite attackers or establishes an exact Judges 18 event.

claims.claim: Judges 18:30 has a Moses/Manasseh issue associated with a suspended Hebrew nun; report textual forms and avoid confidently reconstructing editorial motives.
claims.evidence: Judges 18:30 (Hebrew Bible, Judges 1–21, Masoretic text, read in full in Hebrew and JPS English via Mechon Mamre). In the Hebrew text as printed, the name is written with a nun suspended above the line between the first two letters, turning Mosheh into Manasseh. New English Translation of the Septuagint, Judges (A and B Greek texts), NETS (Oxford University Press, 2007/2009 edition), Judges 18:27–31 read in full: recension A reads "Moyses," while recension B reads "Manasses." The King James Version follows the Masoretic form and reads "Manasseh." Report textual forms only; do not confidently reconstruct editorial motives — the usual explanation (a scribe suspended the nun to protect Moses' reputation) is a probable inference rather than an observed fact. Textual description only; the narrated event is not externally corroborated.

claims.claim: Judges 17 narrates Micah of Mount Ephraim making a household shrine with a carved image and a cast image from two hundred shekels of silver, an ephod and teraphim, first consecrating one of his sons as priest and then hiring a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah for ten shekels of silver a year, clothing and food, and concluding that the LORD will do him good because he has a Levite as priest.
claims.evidence: Judges 17:1–13 (Hebrew Bible, Judges 1–21, Masoretic text, read in full in Hebrew and JPS English via Mechon Mamre; chapter 17 carries no diffs of any class). William G. Dever, "Archaeology and Folk or Family Religion in Ancient Israel," Religions 10(12) (2019), 667, §§2 and 4.4, peer-reviewed, open access, read in full: "folk religion" is usually termed "family" or "household" religion, "the actual, widespread practice of religion at the household level"; "we now have a number of Israelite household shrines" — e.g. a tenth-century "Cult Corner" at Megiddo, a seventh-century domestic shrine on the Jerusalem Ophel, a shrine room at Tel Halif, and houses at Beersheba. These examples are tenth- to seventh-century and do not identify Micah's shrine, date it, or prove the Judges 17 episode; they show only that the kind of installation the text describes — a domestic shrine with cultic objects — is a known Iron Age practice. Textual description only; the narrated event is not externally corroborated.
